entry.title: Rejection Reason in SAP MDG: Less Guessing, Faster Resubmissions
entry.content:
Introduction

When a governance process gets rejected, the requester might be left with one question: why? Without a clear explanation, they will reach out to the approver, wait for a response, and only then fix the issue and resubmit. And all of that could have been avoided with a short note from the approver.

For MDG change requests in classic mode, rejection reasons have been available for a long time. This feature is now also coming to master data processes on SAP Master Data Governance on S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition and is planned for SAP Master Data Governance on S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition 2025 FPS2, cloud-ready mode. 

How it works

When an approver clicks "Reject" or "Send for Revision" from My Inbox-App, a dialog appears asking for a reason. The dialog has two parts:

  • Free text note: the approver needs to write a detailed explanation. This note is added to the process and is visible to the requester.
  • Rejection reasons: if configured, the approver can pick from a drop-down list of rejection reasons. These are defined per process template, so different processes can have different sets of reasons.

If rejection reasons are configured for a process template, both fields become mandatory. There is no way to reject a process without providing at least some explanation. This makes the approval workflow more transparent and cuts down on back-and-forth between approvers and requesters.

Where can you see the rejection reason?

After a process is rejected, the rejection reason appears directly in the process header. The requester does not have to search for it. The free text note is also stored as a process note and can be reviewed at any time.

The rejection reason is also available as a filter option in all process apps, which makes it easier to spot patterns in data quality issues or submission problems.

And it’s also visible for withdrawn and deleted processes:

How to configure rejection reasons

Rejection reasons are configured per process template. For SAP Master Data Governance on S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition this can be done via a Self-Service Configuration UI.  (SSCUI > Database and Data Management > Master Data Governance > Define Process Rejection Reasons)

If no rejection reasons are configured for a process template, the drop-down is not shown. When rejection reasons are configured for a process template, the same dialog also appears when a user tries to delete an active, not yet completed process.

Are you planning to use rejection reasons in your master data processes? We'd love to hear what you think. Share your experience or questions in the comments below!

Availability

  • SAP Master Data Governance on S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition
  • Planned for SAP Master Data Governance on S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition 2025 FPS2, cloud-ready mode

entry.title: Enhancing SAP MDG Workflow Inbox with a Custom Change Request Type (CR Type) Column
entry.content:
Introduction

SAP Master Data Governance (MDG) processes are driven by Change Requests (CRs). Every create, modify, block, unblock, or delete activity is managed through a Change Request workflow.

In one of our MDG implementations, business users raised a common usability concern regarding the MDG Workflow Inbox. Although the standard inbox displays information such as Change Request number, requester, creation date, and workflow status, it does not clearly indicate the purpose of the Change Request.

As a result, approvers and data stewards had to open each workflow item to determine whether it was related to a Create, Modify, Block, Unblock, or Delete process. When dealing with a large volume of workflow items, this additional navigation impacted productivity and slowed down the approval process.

While analyzing the requirement, I explored how the MDG Workflow Inbox retrieves and displays data through the POWL framework. What initially appeared to be a simple UI enhancement turned into a useful learning exercise around POWL feeder classes, result structures, and workflow data enrichment.

In this blog, I will share how I enhanced the standard MDG Workflow Inbox by adding a new column called CR Type, enabling users to identify the purpose of a Change Request directly from the inbox without opening the work item.

Project Context and Lessons Learned

This enhancement originated from a requirement in an MDG environment where business users processed a significant number of Change Requests daily. Regardless of the underlying master data domain, users wanted a quick way to understand the nature of a workflow item before opening it. Their primary expectation was simple: display the Change Request type directly in the inbox so they could prioritize work more effectively.

One aspect that surprised me during implementation was that the enhancement could not be achieved through inbox personalization or simple configuration. Initially, I assumed the required information might already be available in the standard POWL configuration. However, after investigating the framework, I found that the inbox content is driven by the feeder class and its associated result structure. Therefore, introducing a new business field required extending the standard feeder logic.

Another interesting challenge was understanding the relationship between workflow work items and MDG Change Requests. The workflow inbox contains workflow-centric information, while the Change Request Type resides within MDG-specific structures. The enhancement therefore required enriching the result data by mapping workflow items back to their corresponding Change Requests and retrieving the required business information before displaying it in the inbox.

A key takeaway from this implementation was the flexibility offered by the POWL framework. Once the feeder class enhancement pattern was understood, the same approach could be reused to display additional business-relevant attributes in the Workflow Inbox whenever future requirements arise

Business Requirement

Current Issue

Currently, it is not possible to identify the specific Change Request process directly from the Workflow Inbox. Users cannot determine whether a workflow item belongs to:

  • Create
  • Modify
  • Block
  • Unblock
  • Delete

without first opening the Change Request.

Expected Result

Add a new column labeled CR Type to the Workflow Inbox so users can immediately identify the purpose of a Change Request and prioritize their actions accordingly.

Solution Overview

The solution consists of extending the standard POWL feeder class used by the MDG Workflow Inbox and enhancing the inbox result structure with a new field containing the Change Request Type.

High-level implementation steps:

  1. Create a custom structure and table type.
  2. Create a custom feeder class inheriting from the standard feeder class.
  3. Add the CR Type field to the inbox structure.
  4. Populate the CR Type value during result retrieval.
  5. Replace the standard feeder class in POWL configuration.
  6. Display the new column in the Workflow Inbox.

Final Output

After implementation, users can see the Change Request Type directly in the Workflow Inbox without opening the workflow item.

Figure 1: Enhanced SAP MDG Workflow Inbox displaying the newly added CR Type column.

Figure 1: Enhanced Workflow Inbox displaying the CR Type column. Sensitive values have been masked for documentation purposes.

Implementation Details

Step 1: Create a Custom Structure

Create a custom structure by copying the standard inbox structure and adding the required field.

Standard Structure
------------------
USMD_S_CREQUEST_POWL

Custom Structure
----------------
ZMDGF_USMD_S_CREQUEST_POWL

Add the new component:

Create the corresponding custom table type:

Step 2: Create a Custom Feeder Class

Create a custom feeder class inheriting from the standard feeder class.

Class:
ZCL_USMD_CREQUEST_POWL

Super Class:
CL_USMD_CREQUEST_POWL

This custom class will provide the enhanced inbox structure and populate the CR Type field.

Step 3: Redefine Required Methods

Redefine the following methods:

SET_MV_RESULTS

SET_MV_RESULTSTRUCTURE

IF_POWL_FEEDER~GET_OBJECTS

IF_POWL_FEEDER~GET_OBJECT_DEFINITION

Within method SET_MV_RESULTSTRUCTURE, point the inbox to the custom structure.

This allows the Workflow Inbox to recognize and display the additional CR Type column.

Step 4: Populate the CR Type

Redefine method:

IF_POWL_FEEDER~GET_OBJECTS

First call the superclass implementation and then enrich the returned results.

The enhancement logic performs the following activities:

  • Read workflow items from the inbox.
  • Map workflow items to Change Requests.
  • Read Change Request details.
  • Fetch the Change Request Type.
  • Populate field USMD_CRTYPE in the result structure.

The resulting inbox data now contains the Change Request Type for every workflow item.

Step 5: Identify Existing POWL Configuration

Before updating the feeder class, identify the POWL configuration used by the Workflow Inbox.

Execute transaction:

POWL_TYPE

Search for the standard feeder class and note the corresponding:

  • POWL Type ID
  • Query ID
  • Application ID

For this example:

POWL Type ID : USMD_CREQUEST_WI

Query ID : USMD_CREQUEST_WI

Application : FIN_MDM_CREQUEST

Step 6: Replace the Standard Feeder Class

Open transaction:

POWL_TYPE

Locate:

USMD_CREQUEST_WI

Replace the standard feeder class:

CL_USMD_CREQUEST_POWL

with:

ZCL_USMD_CREQUEST_POWL

Save and transport the changes.

Step 7: Verify Component Configuration

Execute transaction:

Verify the Application ID and related component configuration.

If required, create a custom component type:

ZUSMD_TXTMI

This can be used to provide a user-friendly column header:

CR Type

Testing Results

After transporting and activating the enhancement:

  • Workflow Inbox continues to function normally.
  • New CR Type column becomes available.
  • Users can identify Create, Modify, Block, Unblock, and Delete requests directly from the inbox.
  • No additional navigation is required to determine the purpose of the Change Request.

Benefits

  • Improved user experience.
  • Reduced manual navigation.
  • Faster workflow processing.
  • Improved Change Request visibility.
  • Better prioritization of work items.
  • Reusable enhancement framework for future inbox fields.

Important Note

The Workflow Inbox is a common component used across multiple MDG domains. If the standard POWL definition is modified directly, the new column may also become visible in other MDG processes.

If domain-specific behavior is required, consider creating a dedicated role and custom POWL configuration to restrict the enhancement to the intended business area.

Conclusion

Working on this enhancement provided valuable insight into how the MDG Workflow Inbox leverages the POWL framework to retrieve and present workflow data. Although the requirement initially seemed like a straightforward UI improvement, implementing it required a deeper understanding of feeder class inheritance, inbox result structures, and workflow-to-change-request relationships.

By extending the standard MDG Workflow Inbox feeder class and introducing a custom CR Type field, users can now immediately identify the purpose of each Change Request directly from the inbox. This eliminates unnecessary navigation, improves visibility, and helps users process workflow items more efficiently.

Beyond addressing the immediate business requirement, this enhancement also established a reusable framework that can be leveraged to expose additional business information in the MDG Workflow Inbox as new requirements emerge.

entry.title: The Data Nobody Owns: Why Reference Data Deserves Its Own Governance Story
entry.content:
Part 1 of two. This post makes the business case. Part 2 covers how Reference Data Management for SAP MDG works in practice.

A short test

Ask three people in your organization who is allowed to create a new material group. Then ask who checks whether it duplicates an existing one, and who makes sure the new value reaches every system that needs it.

In most organizations, the three answers do not match. Often there is no answer at all for the second question.

That is the situation for reference data in a nutshell. Country codes, material groups, units of measure, company codes, payment terms, document types. Somebody creates them, usually in a customizing transaction, usually because a project needed them by Friday. After that, nobody owns them.

Why this stays invisible for years

Master data gets attention because it moves. Customers change addresses, materials get new suppliers, prices shift. The pain is immediate and somebody feels it.

Reference data barely moves. A material group created in 2014 sits there quietly. Nothing breaks on the day it is created wrong, so nobody looks. The impact shows up somewhere else entirely, and much later.

By the time somebody investigates, the cause is five years old and nobody remembers the decision. Reference data has a low change frequency but a high business impact, because it is used in nearly every business process. That combination is what makes it so easy to underestimate.

What it actually costs

Four cost categories come up again and again.

Slow and unreliable processes. When sales, purchasing, logistics, and finance work with overlapping or divergent reference values, every cross functional step needs a reconciliation loop. Nobody books that as a cost, but it consumes real hours every week.

Commercial risk in operations. Wrong material statuses, unclear storage location definitions, and inconsistent shipping conditions lead to spoiled goods, inefficient storage, and delivery problems. These are not data problems in the ledger. They are physical.

Integration cost in projects. This is the one finance notices. Every time a system is connected, acquired, or migrated, somebody has to map reference values by hand. The cost scales with the mess, and it gets paid again in the next project.

Decisions on unreliable reports. Analytics built on inconsistent reference data produce numbers that look precise and are not. The reporting layer cannot repair what the source never agreed on. This is the same argument that is currently being made about AI readiness, and it applies here first.

What the target state looks like

The target state is easy to describe and harder to reach: one place where reference data is defined, one process for changing it, and one path by which changes reach every system that needs them. Three things change when that is in place.

Reference data gets an owner. Not a system, a person. Data stewards decide what is correct, data specialists know the naming rules and technical constraints, requesters can ask for what they need without knowing either. Responsibility moves out of the customizing transaction and into a defined process.

Every value carries its meaning. A material group is not just a key with a short text. It can carry the usage scenario, the rules for when to apply it, the person to ask. Attach that documentation to the value itself and it stays available to the next colleague who wonders whether to reuse or create. This sounds like a footnote. In practice it is often the difference between a catalog people use and a catalog people bypass.

Distribution becomes traceable. When a new value is approved, the systems that receive it are defined in advance rather than remembered by whoever happens to be involved, and it is visible whether the change arrived. The distribution itself still has to be set up, but it stops being something an individual has to remember.

Two capabilities, in the right order

Getting there involves two distinct capabilities, and the order matters more than most projects expect.

First, harmonize. Find out what actually exists across your systems today, decide which values are the correct ones, and bring the systems into alignment. This is unglamorous work and it produces no new functionality. It is also the only foundation on which the rest can stand.

Then, govern. Once the values are aligned, put a process around changing it, so it stays that way. Approval steps, clear roles, automatic distribution, an audit trail.

Doing this in reverse is the most common failure mode. A governance process wrapped around inconsistent data does not fix the inconsistency. It formalizes it, adds approval steps, and gives everyone the impression that the problem is handled.

The useful consequence: harmonization can start before any governance tooling is in place, and it delivers value on its own. Reference Data Management for SAP MDG reflects this in its structure, with harmonization available as a separate capability that does not require MDG at all.

One decision to make consciously

There is a question every organization has to answer, and it is not a technical one: who controls when a reference data change reaches production?

Two legitimate answers exist. IT can control it, with the change moving through the usual development, test, and production stages. Or the business can control it, with an approved change going into the productive systems directly, governed by the approval workflow instead of the transport process.

The first gives you a test cycle. The second gives you speed. Most organizations need both, applied to different objects, and the good news is that the choice can be made per object rather than once for everything. What matters is that it is a deliberate decision, made with the process owners in the room, and not an accident of how the first object happened to be configured. Part 2 goes into how both paths work.

Where to start

If this describes your landscape, three steps are worth taking before any tooling discussion:

  1. Pick five objects that hurt. Not the full catalog. The ones where you already know inconsistency is costing you, typically material group, unit of measure, payment terms, or plant related values.
  2. Find out what exists. Extract the current values from every relevant system and compare. The result of this exercise is usually the strongest argument you will have for the business case.
  3. Name owners before naming tools. A stewardship model on paper, agreed with the process owners, is worth more than a governance workflow with nobody accountable behind it.

Key takeaways

  • Reference data changes rarely and is used everywhere. That is what makes it easy to ignore and expensive to ignore.
  • The cost shows up as reconciliation effort, integration project overhead, and unreliable reporting, rarely under a line item called reference data.
  • Harmonize first, govern second. Governance applied to inconsistent data formalizes the inconsistency.
  • Ownership is an organizational question. Tooling supports it, it does not create it.

How is reference data handled in your organization: owned by a named team, or created by whoever needs it first? I would like to hear how others have made the case for investing here.

Part 2 will cover the solution side: how governance and harmonization work in Reference Data Management for SAP MDG, the two distribution paths into production, and how to keep the scope under control.

entry.title: What's new in Master Data Governance in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition 2608?
entry.content:
Hello and welcome back to my blog post! Happy to have you here!

I'm thrilled to walk you through the latest Master Data Governance enhancements from our SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition 2608 release.

Central Governance of Product Data and Central Governance of Business Partners, including customer and supplier segments

In the fast-paced digital economy, the quality of your master data is not just an IT concern - it's the bedrock of your entire enterprise. Poor data can lead to inefficiencies in your supply chain, inaccuracies in planning, and missed opportunities with customers. With the SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition 2608 release, we are introducing powerful new central governance capabilities that empower you to take full control of your most critical data assets. These features are essential for master data stewards, business process owners, and any leader who understands that trusted data drives better business outcomes.

 

Lets dive into the highlights.


Key Highlights


Central Governance of Product Data


Imagine creating and maintaining your product master records with a process that is not only efficient but also ensures complete accuracy and compliance from the very beginning. With the new central governance for product data, this is now your reality. We’re providing a governed, workflow-driven approach to manage the entire lifecycle of your product data.

This new capability allows you to enforce data quality right at the point of entry. Now you can:
- Govern data with workflows to involve all stakeholders every time, ensuring transparency and collaboration.
- Implement configurable validation rules to embed your unique business logic and ensure data consistency alongside native S/4HANA checks.
- Automate field value derivation to reduce manual effort and increase accuracy from the moment data is created.
- Perform mass updates across multiple product records, making data maintenance significantly more efficient, even for the largest datasets.

The business value is clear: Better product data leads to better outcomes across your planning, production, and supply chain processes.

 

Create an entry in Central GovernanceView General Information of Created Product

 

Central Governance of Business Partners


Your relationships with customers and suppliers are your most valuable assets. The new central governance for business partners ensures the data underpinning these relationships is always accurate, complete, and trustworthy. This feature provides a governed, workflow-driven method for creating and maintaining business partners, including their relationships and specific customer and supplier roles.

This helps teams by centralizing control and improving data quality across the board. Now you can:
- Utilize workflow-driven data entry for all business partner central data, including supplier and customer segments at the company code, purchasing organization, and sales area levels.
- Ingest trusted information directly from external data providers, such as company names, addresses, and tax ID numbers, to reduce manual entry and errors.
- Leverage flexible workflows through integration with SAP Build Process Automation, tailoring approval processes to your exact organizational needs.
- Integrate external data creation and updates through seamless inbound processing.

By enforcing data quality with robust validation and derivation rules, you ensure that every business process that relies on partner data - from procurement to sales - is running on a foundation of trust.

These new features in SAP Master Data Governance represent a major step forward in building a truly intelligent and sustainable enterprise. By establishing a single source of truth for your product and business partner data, you unlock new levels of efficiency, compliance, and strategic agility.

entry.title: Integrating SAP Concur with SAP SuccessFactors using MDI
entry.content:
SAP Concur can be integrated with SAP SuccessFactors in several ways, ranging from traditional file-based interfaces to modern API-driven integrations. Each approach has its own strengths and trade-offs, making the optimal choice dependent on the customer's landscape, integration requirements, and long-term strategy.

This post builds on previously covered integration options and takes a deeper dive into the Master Data Integration (MDI) approach. MDI provides a standardized approach to maintaining consistent, high-quality master data between SAP SuccessFactors, SAP Concur, and other SAP solutions, making it a key component of SAP's cloud integration strategy.

Prerequisites

Before beginning the configuration, ensure the following foundational components are in place:

  • An active SAP BTP Commercial License (CPEA or PAYG contract) - Needed for subscribing to SAP Master Data Integration)
  • An SAP SuccessFactors Employee Central tenant configured as the employee data provider
  • An SAP Concur tenant with appropriate administrative access
  • Access to SAP Cloud Identity Services (Identity Authentication Service / Identity Provisioning Service)
  • Access to SAP Cloud ALM for monitoring (optional but highly recommended for Customer Monitoring)
  • The Master Data Integration Administrator and Intelligent Enterprise Suite (IES) Integrations Administrator role assigned in SAP Concur

Integration Steps

Step 1 — Set Up Integration Between SuccessFactors - Cloud identity services - Concur

Raise a support ticket through the Concur Support Portal or SAP Portal to configure your SAP IAS/IPS tenant. When raising the ticket, explicitly mention that you are implementing MDI with SAP Concur, as the relevant roles can be assigned at once.

  • If using ServiceNow, use component BNS-CON-MDI-UPS for SAP Concur Integration with SAP Master Data Integration Service
  • If using the Concur support tool, reference the issue as IPS Provisioning
  • Always include your SAP Customer Number in the ticket (see here for more details)

Once the Intelligent Enterprise Suite (IES) Integrations Administrator role has been assigned by Concur personnel, trigger the automation and adjust the IAS configuration as needed. In some cases, IAS acts as a proxy rather than a direct identity provider, and configuration adjustments — such as the Subject Name Identifier — may be required.

Step 2 — Review and Adjust IPS Jobs

Review the jobs automatically created in the Identity Provisioning Service (IPS) and adjust them as needed.

The following guides might be helpful in configuring the source and target systems.

IPS is primarily used to provision the "user core" — basic user information such as name, login ID, employee ID, and email address. Expense and Travel-related profile data (such as organizational units, ledger, and employee group) are populated by MDI in a later step.

Important: You will also need an IPS job to assign roles, including the Approver role — a permission that allows users to approve expense reports, typically granted to managers. This can be managed via a dedicated group in IPS, synchronized from SuccessFactors based on criteria such as job code.

User core and the Approver role cannot be assigned simultaneously if the user does not yet exist in Concur. Therefore, the IPS job will need to be re-run after MDI has populated the Expense-related data.

Step 3 — Configure SuccessFactors–MDI Integration

This step involves:

  • Creating a BTP Service Instance for SuccessFactors
  • Creating MDI subaccount and configuring it including a service instance creation (in case customer does not have MDI yet)
  • Configure Business Scenario - Workforce Replication from EC to SAP Master Data Integration
  • Establishing the correct field mapping in the SuccessFactors–MDI configuration
  • Starting the replication from SuccessFactors to MDI

Refer to the official SAP Help documentation on Integrating SAP SuccessFactors Employee Central with SAP Master Data Integration for detailed how-to guidance.

Step 4 — Create Formation Between MDI and SAP Concur (BTP)

In this step, create a formation in SAP BTP between the SAP Master Data Integration Service and SAP Concur Solutions to establish connectivity.

  • The MDI Tenant and Concur Tenant should be auto-discovered. If they are not, raise a support case.
  • Two communication paths are established:
    • Concur → MDI Communication
    • BDO (Business Data Orchestration) → Concur Communication

Refer to the SAP Help documentation on Creating a Formation Between the SAP Master Data Integration Service and SAP Concur Solutions to Establish Connectivity for step-by-step instructions.

Step 5 — Configure SAP Cloud ALM (CALM) Monitoring

Set up SAP Cloud ALM in SAP BTP and activate monitoring for SAP Concur.

This step is essential for ongoing visibility into synchronization status and errors.

Step 6 — Field Mapping and Role Assignment

If the Master Data Integration Administrator role has not yet been assigned in SAP Concur, raise a support case to request the assignment.

This role  provides access to the Field Mapping configuration page in SAP Concur, where you can:

  • Define the mapping of ODM fields to Concur fields
  • Apply Implementation Codes, Conversion Codes, or Value Mappings as required

Review the Default Field Mapping documentation to understand out-of-the-box mappings and determine any custom mappings required for your organization.

Step 7 — Configure Business Data Orchestration (BDO) Distribution Model

In this step:

  • Create a Distribution Model for the existing Workforce Person object in the BDO service
  • Configure the distribution model by setting:
    • Activate the BDO distribution model to start the replication
    • Business Object (Workforce Person)
    • Filters (e.g., object selection criteria)
    • Frequency (scheduling for replication)

Step 8 — Initial Test Run

Before triggering a full load:

  • Add only a few employee IDs to the Object Selection Filter in the BDO service
  • Trigger IPS job to create "user core" before triggering MDI
  • Trigger initial load (for subsequent tests use delta replication - delta will be triggered if there are changes made in SuccessFactors)
  • Monitor SAP Cloud ALM for synchronization errors before proceeding with a broader rollout

Key Hints & Best Practices

  • Scheduling: Ensure the IPS job used to create the user core runs before MDI. The IPS job responsible for provisioning Approver roles must run after MDI — this can be the same job used for user core provisioning or a separate dedicated job. Sequencing is critical to avoid provisioning failures.
  • Monitoring: Actively monitor both IPS jobs and SAP Cloud ALM for errors. Error logs are not displayed in the Concur UI, so external monitoring is the only way to detect and resolve issues in a timely manner.
  • Troubleshooting: When engaging SAP Concur support for error analysis, always provide:
    • The Correlation ID of the request
    • The timeframe of the issue (a date is sufficient if Correlation ID is present)
    • A downloaded copy of the error message

Conclusion

Master Data Integration (MDI) provides a modern and standardized approach to synchronizing master data between SAP SuccessFactors and SAP Concur. By centralizing data distribution and leveraging SAP Cloud ALM (CALM) for monitoring and observability, organizations can improve data consistency, simplify integration management, and reduce administrative effort.

A successful implementation depends on three key factors: establishing a solid identity provisioning process with IAS and IPS, ensuring the correct sequence of user creation and role assignment, and defining accurate mappings for expense-related master data.

When implementing MDI, it is recommended to begin with a small pilot group, closely monitor synchronization jobs in IPS and SAP Cloud ALM, and fine-tune mappings and scheduling before expanding the integration to the entire organization. Following these best practices will help you build a reliable, scalable, and maintainable integration that provides a strong foundation for SAP Concur travel and expense processes.

entry.title: SAP Master Data Governance on SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition · Release 2608 - Highlights
entry.content:
SAP Master Data Governance on S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition - Central Governance for Products arrives and more

SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, master data governance · Release 2608 Highlights

The Bigger Picture: Autonomous Enterprise, BDC, and the Role of Master Data

SAP's vision of the Autonomous Enterprise puts AI at the heart of every business process - intelligent agents that sense, decide, and act with minimal human intervention. That vision only works if the underlying data is trustworthy. SAP Business Data Cloud (BDC) provides the unified data fabric: it centralizes, harmonizes, and enriches master, transactional, and third-party data from SAP and non-SAP systems into a single, governed source of truth. SAP Master Data Governance (MDG) is the quality gate at the origin - ensuring that every record entering BDC and every downstream AI agent starts from a solid data foundation.

SAP Master Data Governance on S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition is the right choice for organizations running their ERP in SAP's public cloud. It delivers governed creation, change, and distribution of business partner and product master data - consumer-grade user experience, standardized APIs, embedded AI, and now, with this release, a central governance capability for the product data domain.

What's New in Release 2608

Release 2608 of SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, master data governance delivers a set of tightly focused innovations that extend governance depth, increase automation, and improve the day-to-day experience for master data stewards and business users alike. The headline: Central Governance for Product is available for the first time. Alongside that, AI-based natural language filtering, data-provider integration for business partner governance, and central governance for Business Partners now completed with customer and supplier segments round out a meaningful release.

Central Governance for Product — Available for the First Time in Public Cloud

This is the milestone of this release. Until now, SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, master data governance offered consolidation, mass processing, and data quality management for product data. Central governance - the controlled, workflow-driven creation and change of individual product records at the point of origin - was missing.  Release 2608 closes that gap offering a dedicated suite of Fiori apps enabling business users and master data stewards to request, validate, approve, and activate product master data through a governed process.

Visit SAP What's New Viewer Central Governance Apps for Product for further insights.

New Fiori Apps Delivered

The following apps are new with release 2608 for central governance of product data:

App

App ID

What it does

Manage Products – Central Governance

F8467

Single entry point to create, display, and edit product master data

Manage Governance Processes - Products

F8466

Create and display governance processes, including mass processes

Mass Edit Central Governance - Products

F8468

Create and display mass governance processes for product data

Track Changes - Products

F8469

Display all products touched by a finalized governance process

View Summary of Changes - Products

F8470

Monitor field-level changes; accessible from any activated process

Export Master Data – Products

F8465

Export a selection of product master data to a local file

Manage Inbound Processes - Products

F9381

Organize de-central creation and change processes for product data

 

Use Central Governance by enabling Feature: MDC_PRODUCT_GOVERNANCE 

This feature will not automatically be available in your system but requires that you activate the feature Successor MDG Apps for Product (MDC_PRODUCT_GOVERNANCE) in the configuration activity Activate Features as described in the documentation  (For more information, see  Activate Features).

Using this feature requires an additional license for SAP Master Data Governance in addition to your usage right for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. It extends the functionality provided with scope item Mass Processing for Product (1N5) to provide central governance capabilities. Do not activate this feature if you are only using the functionality of scope item Mass Load and Mass Maintenance for Product (1RM).

Activating this new feature has the following effects:

  • You can use the new mode apps.
  • You can use neither the previous mode apps for consolidation and mass processing nor any of the related apps such as Export Master Data, Import Master Data, and Track Changes.
  • Processes created in the previous mode can be continued in the new mode.
  • Processes created in the old mode cannot be rolled back to their initial step because the related process template is no longer available.
  • In Mass Processing, including Mass Load and Mass Maintenance, you work with a reduced scope of the product data model  when updating in UI. 

Activating the new mode, for example for test reasons, and then deactivating it again has the following effects: 

  • Processes created in the new mode cannot be continued in the previous mode. This scenario is not supported. 
  • The previous mode apps can be used. 
  • The new mode apps cannot be used. 

Note:  This feature is reversible. 


Standard Process Flow

The standard template follows a dual-control design: the requester submits the product data; the approver reviews it in read-only mode and cannot change the data during approval. Workflow capabilities are optional and can be activated as needed. At the end of the process, data replication is triggered automatically. Email notifications inform the requester of the approval or rejection outcome.

▲ BTP-integrated approval workflow log for Create Product


The Create Product Experience

The Manage Products - Central Governance app (F8467) allows you to search and author product data. The search screen supports configurable filters, cross-field search, saved views, and direct export of hit lists to spreadsheet - familiar interaction patterns.

▲ Manage Products search & filter UI with save-view and export capabilities


Creating a new product starts with a Quick Create popup for the most important header fields, followed by a full master data form. Drafts are saved automatically. Users can submit inline or continue editing before submission.

▲ Quick Create popup and full product maintenance form - 3-step interaction flow

▲ Product maintenance UI showing all process actions, validation feedback, and submission controls

Built-in Duplicate Check

The user can start an integrated duplicate check based on rules defined in the Self-Service Configuration UI (SSCU). If potential duplicates are found, users can navigate directly to the duplicate record via smart link - preventing redundant products before they reach the active area.

▲ Duplicate check result with smart link navigation to the existing product


Notes, Classification, and Texts

Process notes are available in the header of every governance app - users can write context notes and read existing ones throughout the process lifecycle. Product classification assigns materials to their material classes directly within the governance UI. Long text (plain) can be created and edited; existing formatted long text is displayed read-only.

▲ Process notes available in the header of all governance process apps

▲ Notes entry panel — maintain description, due date, and free-text notes per process

▲ Assign products to material classification classes directly within central governance

Track Changes — Full Audit Trail

Two dedicated apps give a complete audit trail. Track Changes - Products (F8469) lists, at process level, all products that were changed as part of a finalized governance process. View Summary of Changes - Products (F8470) then drills into field-level detail for any activated product - who changed what, and when.

▲ Track Changes Step 1 - process-level list of changed business objects

▲ Track Changes Step 2 - field-level change detail per product

 

Business Partner Central Governance — Enhanced UX and Process Transparency

Central Governance for Business Partner (scope item 1N7) receives a meaningful UX upgrade in release 2608. The focus is on closing the last friction points between how stewards work and how the system supports them:

Notes: Notes on all processes - write and read process context notes in any governance, consolidation, or mass-processing  workflow.

Priority: Choose from a configurable list of priorities.

Due Date: Process header data - maintain a description and due date on every process for better workload visibility.

Reason: Choose from a configurable list of reasons.

▲ Enhanced Process Transparency showing more fields in Process Data

Rejection Reason: When an approver clicks "Reject" or "Send for Revision" from My Inbox-App, a dialog appears asking for a reason. The dialog has two parts:

Free text note: the approver needs to write a detailed explanation. This note is added to the process and is visible to the requester.

Rejection reason: if configured, the approver can pick from a drop-down list of rejection reasons. These are defined per process template, so different processes can have different sets of reasons.

▲ Rejection Reason: Also visible for withdrawn and deleted processes.

Data Provider Integration — Trusted Reference Data at the Point of Entry

Central Governance for Business Partner

Data quality starts at the moment of creation. S/4HANA Public Cloud 2608 introduces configurable external data provider integration directly into the business partner governance workflow. When a steward creates or changes a business partner record, they can select from multiple configured external providers - address validators, VAT registries or any other approved source - look up reference data from the chosen provider, and review the full context before pulling it in.

The key benefits: reuse proven, cleansed reference data instead of rekeying it, reduce manual errors, and accelerate data entry. Multiple providers can be configured in parallel for different use cases or regions. Each provider's availability and data quality status is visible directly in the workflow, so stewards always know what they're working with.

Please read also following post: Bring your own Data Provider to SAP Master Data Governance.

▲ Reference data from external provider populated into the governance form

▲ Reference Record Object Page: review provider status and full record details before creating a business partner

What Comes Next

This release is a significant step - but the roadmap keeps moving. Extended Joule integration for Master Data Governance processes (AI-assisted validation rule creation, Joule-driven data provider enrichment) is planned for the upcoming Q1 release per SAP Roadmap Explorer. Data model extensions for business partner and further coverage of the product central governance domain are also on the horizon.

For organizations using SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, the release 2608 delivers the governance foundation to keep product and business partner data accurate, governed, and AI-ready - right at the point of entry. The best time to put this in place is before the data problems arrive.

entry.title: The Most Important Part of Supplier Validation Wasn't the Technology: A Governance Lesson
entry.content:
Introduction

Many organisations investing in ERP transformation, automation and AI recognise the importance of high-quality master data.

Yet supplier onboarding and maintenance often remain heavily dependent on manual checks, inconsistent standards and local interpretation.

During a supplier validation exercise, I was reminded of a lesson I have seen repeatedly throughout finance systems projects:

Technology can improve data quality, but only if the organisation first agrees what "good" looks like.

The technical solution was relatively straightforward.

The governance lesson was much more valuable.

The Business Problem

Like many organisations, supplier master data had evolved over time from a variety of sources.

Although suppliers had company names and registration numbers recorded, the data was not always consistent with official records.

Examples included:

  • Abbreviated legal names
  • Historical company names
  • Data entry errors
  • Missing company registration numbers
  • Inconsistencies between supplier records and external sources

None of these issues were individually significant.

Collectively, however, they created challenges for:

  • Supplier validation
  • Reporting
  • Supplier onboarding
  • Duplicate detection
  • Future automation opportunities

The risk was not simply poor data quality.

The greater risk was that future controls and automation would be built on unreliable foundations.

Improving Data Quality Before the Long-Term Solution

A common response to master data issues is:

"The new ERP process will solve it."

In reality, business challenges rarely wait for roadmap delivery.

While SAP provides strong capabilities around Business Partner governance, master data management and validation, the need to improve data quality often exists long before a future-state solution is available.

The objective was therefore not to replace future capabilities.

The objective was to improve data quality immediately while remaining aligned to sound governance principles.

That distinction proved important.

A Pragmatic Validation Approach

The validation began with an extract from SAP using the Display Supplier List app. The app was already available and configured, so it provided a pragmatic starting point without requiring additional SAP development.

For each supplier, the extract included:

  • NAME1 and NAME2, containing the supplier name
  • STCD3, containing the UK company registration number

For UK suppliers, the principal comparisons were:

  • SAP NAME1 + NAME2 against the registered company name returned by Companies House
  • SAP STCD3 against the Companies House company number

For other countries or localisations, additional SAP name fields such as NAME3 and NAME4 may be required to represent the full legal name. The approach described here was specifically designed around UK-registered companies and should not be assumed to apply unchanged in other jurisdictions.

Power Query submitted the company registration number held in STCD3 to the Companies House API. Where a matching record was returned, the query retrieved:

  • The registered company name
  • The company status
The returned company name was then compared with the supplier name constructed from NAME1 and NAME2 after normalisation.

The objective was deliberately narrow. The process did not perform full supplier due diligence or determine whether a supplier should be commercially approved. It validated selected legal-entity information held in SAP against an authoritative UK company register.

Validation Rules and Normalisation

 

Before comparison, both the SAP supplier name and the Companies House company name were normalised to reduce false exceptions caused by common formatting differences.

The normalisation included:

  • Converting all text to upper case
  • Trimming leading and trailing spaces
  • Replacing "&" with "AND"
  • Replacing "+" with "AND"
  • Standardising common legal suffixes:
    • LIMITED → LTD
    • PUBLIC LIMITED COMPANY → PLC
    • LIMITED LIABILITY PARTNERSHIP → LLP
    • LIMITED PARTNERSHIP → LP
  • Removing punctuation and special characters
  • Collapsing multiple spaces into a single space

Company registration numbers were also normalised before being submitted to Companies House by:

  • Removing spaces and hyphens
  • Converting values to upper case
  • Applying the standard Companies House company-number format

The objective was not to make different companies appear identical. It was to ensure that insignificant formatting differences did not prevent an otherwise valid match.
Figure 1: UK supplier validation process using SAP supplier data and Companies House as the external reference source. Supplier records are validated using the company registration number stored in STCD3, with exceptions raised where company details cannot be matched, names do not align after normalisation, or company status requires review.

Rule 1: Company Number Match

The value held in STCD3 was submitted to Companies House as the primary lookup key.

Where the API did not return a matching company record, the supplier was reported as an exception for manual investigation.

A failed match was not automatically treated as proof that the company number was invalid. It could indicate:

  • Incorrect or incomplete data in STCD3
  • A formatting issue
  • A missing leading zero
  • A supplier that was not a UK-registered company
  • A record requiring a different validation route

Rule 2: Legal Name Alignment

Where the company number produced a match, the normalised Companies House company name was compared with the normalised value constructed from NAME1 and NAME2.

If the names matched after normalisation, the supplier passed the name check.

If the names did not match, the supplier was reported as an exception for manual investigation.

Potential explanations included:

  • An incorrect supplier name
  • An historic company name
  • Use of a trading name rather than the registered legal name
  • The legal name being incomplete across the SAP name fields
  • A genuine change to the registered company details

The automated process identified the difference. It did not automatically overwrite the SAP supplier record.

Rule 3: Company Status Review

The company status returned by Companies House was also evaluated.

Where the status was considered appropriate, the supplier could pass the status check.

Where the status was unexpected or potentially concerning, the supplier was reported for manual investigation.

The tool did not automatically determine the action to take against the supplier. The appropriate response depended on the business context and could require further investigation before any controlled SAP master-data change was made.

 

Exception-Based Decision Process

The decision process can be summarised as follows:

  1. Extract supplier information from SAP.
  2. Combine NAME1 and NAME2 for the supplier name.
  3. Read the company registration number from STCD3.
  4. Submit STCD3 to the Companies House API.
  5. If no company is returned, create an exception for manual investigation.
  6. If a company is returned, retrieve the registered name and company status.
  7. Normalise both company names.
  8. If the names do not align, create an exception.
  9. If the company status is unexpected, create an exception.
  10. Investigate and resolve exceptions through the appropriate controlled process.

This separation between automated validation and manual decision-making was important. The technology identified records requiring attention, while investigation and any resulting SAP master-data changes remained controlled activities.


The Unexpected Lesson

Initially, most discussions focused on the technology.

Questions included:

  • Which API should be used?
  • How often should validation run?
  • How should exceptions be reported?

What eventually mattered most was a much simpler question:

What should a consistently validated supplier record actually look like?

For UK-registered suppliers, a straightforward standard was agreed:

The supplier legal name and company registration number should align with the Companies House record.

That single standard created clarity.

Validation became easier.

Exceptions became easier to explain.

Correction activities became more consistent.

Most importantly, everyone was working towards the same outcome.

Figure 2: Governance before automation. An agreed data standard provides the foundation for validation rules, exception management and trusted supplier data. Automation and controls are most effective when built on clearly defined standards.

Why Data Standards Matter More Than Technology

This experience reinforced a pattern I have seen across finance systems projects.

Automation often receives more attention than data standards.

However:

  • Automation scales good processes.
  • Automation also scales poor processes.

Without agreement on data standards:

  • Exception volumes increase
  • Manual intervention increases
  • Reconciliations become harder
  • Trust in automated controls decreases

The validation process identified discrepancies.

The agreed standard determined how those discrepancies were resolved.

In practice, the standard delivered more value than the technology itself.

Before and After

Before

  • Supplier details reviewed individually
  • Company names used as the principal reference
  • Formatting differences created ambiguity
  • Company status required separate investigation
  • Manual effort spread across the full population
  • Interpretations could vary between reviewers

After

  • Supplier population extracted consistently using the Display Supplier List app
  • STCD3 company number used as the primary lookup key
  • Defined normalisation handled capitalisation, punctuation and legal suffix variations
  • Company status returned as part of the API query
  • Manual effort focused on exceptions
  • Exceptions assessed against defined and explainable rules

The improvement was therefore not the removal of manual judgement.

It was the ability to apply consistent validation across the supplier population and focus judgement on records that genuinely required investigation.


How This Relates to SAP Master Data Governance

One of the core objectives of SAP Master Data Governance (MDG) is to establish trusted master data through defined processes, ownership and controls.

Although this exercise did not use SAP MDG, the governance lessons aligned closely with broader MDG principles:

  • Clear ownership of supplier data
  • Defined standards for legal-entity information
  • Repeatable validation rules
  • Exception-based review
  • Controlled correction of master data
  • Use of an authoritative external reference source

The technology may vary, but the governance principles remain remarkably consistent.

Whether validation occurs through Power Query and an external API, an onboarding workflow or an enterprise MDG solution, the same challenge remains:

Agree the standard first. Then automate it.

Lessons Learned

  1. An authoritative external source is valuable, but only if clear rules exist for how discrepancies will be handled.
  2. Supplier master data issues are often process and ownership issues rather than technology issues.
  3. Small improvements in data governance can create a strong foundation for future automation.
  4. The most important design decisions are often the simplest ones.

Conclusion

The most important outcome of this supplier validation exercise was not the technology.

It was the agreement that supplier records should align to an authoritative source and be maintained consistently.

The exercise reinforced a lesson that I believe applies equally to ERP programmes, automation initiatives and AI adoption:

Poor data quality is rarely a technology problem.

More often, it is a standards and governance problem.

Technology can enforce standards at scale.

It cannot define those standards.

Defining and maintaining them remains a governance responsibility.

Note: The exact use of SAP name fields and tax-number fields depends on organisational configuration and localisation. The mappings described in this article reflect a UK validation exercise and should be reviewed before being applied elsewhere.

entry.title: What SAP Reltio in SAP Business Data Cloud means for your data
entry.content:
The MDM gap just got closed: What SAP Reltio in SAP Business Data Cloud means for your data

For anyone who has spent time in the master data trenches, you know the frustration. You have customer records in SAP, more in Salesforce, a few living in Oracle or JD Edwards, and every team swears theirs is the authoritative version. SAP Master Data Governance (MDG) worked beautifully inside the SAP boundary. But the moment a non-SAP system entered the picture; the path forward was rarely straightforward. It is a well-understood limitation, and one that SAP customers have been navigating for years.

That is why the availability of SAP Reltio in SAP Business Data Cloud (BDC) matters. Not as a product launch announcement. As an actual answer.

What SAP Reltio actually does (in plain language)

Think of SAP Reltio as a cloud-native platform that brings your most critical business data, whether that is customers, suppliers, products, or locations, into a single, continuously reconciled view. Every system and team that needs that clean, unified data can access it. It serves as a trusted, multidomain foundation of 360-degree views that business teams, data products, and AI agents can all draw from to operate with confidence.

For data professionals, that description should land differently than the usual master data management (MDM) pitch. It is not a governance layer bolted onto a particular application. It is not a master data quality tool for IT. It is purpose-built for the people who live in the data every day, the stewards, the analysts, and the architects who are responsible for keeping it reliable.

Two different jobs, one complete architecture

SAP Master Data Governance has a well-defined role: governing master data at the SAP core. It enforces policies, drives validation and approval workflows, and maintains data stewardship inside core business processes. For SAP-centric creation scenarios, it does exactly what it was designed to do.

SAP Reltio fills a different role. Where MDG governs data at the point of entry, SAP Reltio unifies it enterprise-wide, building trusted 360-degree views across master data domains. It takes records from across the diverse system landscape, identifies which records represent the same real-world entity, and consolidates them into a complete profile. That profile is then available to any downstream system or tool that needs it.

These are complementary by design. MDG governs the SAP core. SAP Reltio connects and enriches across the enterprise. Together inside BDC, they form a complete MDM architecture rather than two competing answers to the same question.

Why SAP Reltio in BDC changes the equation

SAP Business Data Cloud is only as powerful as the data that flows through it, and that starts with master data. SAP Reltio in BDC adds the unification and entity resolution layer that turns fragmented records from across your landscape into something interesting and something you can act on.

The practical example that resonates with most data teams: a customer exists in SAP, another record for the same customer lives in Salesforce, and no one agrees on which one is right. SAP Reltio's AI-driven entity resolution handles that matching without requiring you to manually configure complex rule sets. The platform uses pre-trained models to identify and unify records across sources, in real time.

That real-time capability is worth pausing on. SAP Reltio delivers continuously validated, curated data at millisecond speeds, meaning AI agents and analytics are always operating on a trusted, up-to-date view of the business rather than a snapshot that is already out of date by the time it is consumed. Whether your use case demands real-time precision or enterprise-scale, the underlying principle is the same: continuously governed, high-quality data that the rest of the business can depend on.

The connection to AI that most teams are missing

Here is the part that matters most if your organization is working toward AI-driven operations or deploying AI agents. An autonomous agent does not stop to question whether a vendor record is a duplicate or whether two customer records refer to the same person. It just acts. If the underlying data is fragmented, inconsistent, or stale, the agent makes wrong decisions at machine speed and scale.

Trusted master data is not a nice-to-have precondition for AI. It is the requirement. SAP MDG and SAP Reltio together in BDC directly address what the data shows is the number one barrier to AI and analytics at scale: bad data (and we know the most business-critical data is master data). The result is a system of context and unified view of the business that AI agents, Joule, and analytics tools can rely on.

What this means for data stewards and MDM practitioners

If you are managing master data today, the questions worth asking are straightforward. Where does your data actually live? How many systems are creating records for the same entities? And when something downstream breaks, whether it is a failed report, a flawed AI output, or a compliance gap, how long does it take you to trace it back to the source?

The crosswalk visibility in SAP Reltio, seeing exactly how records from different systems were resolved into a single consolidated profile, and which source contributed what, gives data stewards a level of transparency that used to require stitching together multiple reports from multiple tools.

The bigger picture

The data quality problem does not live in one system. It spans your entire landscape. And until you have a solution that spans that landscape too, you are managing symptoms rather than the root cause.

SAP Master Data Governance governs master data at the SAP core. SAP Reltio unifies it across every system. Together in SAP Business Data Cloud, they give data professionals a complete architecture for creating, governing, and continuously improving the data that everything else depends on.

If data quality and data trust are on your agenda, this is where the conversation starts.

To find out more about SAP Reltio and master data management solutions at SAP, go to https://www.sap.com/products/data-cloud/master-data-management.html.

entry.title: Connected Data Is Not the Same as Trusted Data
entry.content:
The same customer exists in your CRM, your ERP, and the platform that arrived with an acquisition. Three records, three spellings, three addresses, and nothing linking them. Each system is correct within its own walls.

A person knows how to reconcile them. An AI agent does not. It takes one record, acts on it, and reports back with complete confidence.

That's the challenge we're tackling in Module 2 of the Getting Started with SAP Business Data Cloud series.

Connecting those systems doesn't solve the problem. A pipeline can move records from one system to another, but it doesn't determine whether two records represent the same real-world entity, or which version of the data should be trusted. Something has to sit between connected data and AI to resolve those differences and create a single, trusted view.

That's the role of master data management (MDM). And it's the difference between data you have connected and data you can confidently put an agent on.

In this session, we'll explore how master data management works inside SAP Business Data Cloud, delivered through SAP Master Data Governance and SAP Reltio.

SAP Master Data Governance governs master data at the point of creation across customers, suppliers, and products, tied directly to your SAP Cloud ERP processes. SAP Reltio unifies data from SAP and non-SAP sources, resolving entities at ecosystem scale and publishing them as unified data products.

What we'll explore

During the session, we'll show you how to:

  • Resolve duplicate records across SAP and non-SAP systems into a single golden record
  • Apply survivorship rules to determine which source system wins, and understand why
  • Trace every value in a trusted record back to the system that supplied it
  • Publish unified master data as unified data products that agents and applications can depend on

The demo follows one customer fragmented across seven source systems, including ERP, CRM, IT service management, support, contract management, and third-party data.

You'll see AI-powered matching surface duplicates that rules-based approaches can miss. You'll see the audit trail reconstruct exactly what merged and when. And you'll watch the relationship graph fill in as information from different sources comes together.

Most importantly, you'll see where the final record comes from. Every attribute traces back to a source that already had it. Nobody types the golden record; it is assembled.

An agent is only as reliable as the record behind it. Connectivity gives AI more data. Master data management helps determine which data it can trust.

entry.title: Creating a New Product with "Manage Products - Central Governance" with SAP MDG
entry.content:
Want to see how the new product central governance app works in practice? We’ve published a new video where we walk you through a practical, end-to-end example of creating a new product using MDG in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition.
The scenario showcases a sample governance flow with request and approval steps ensuring clean, consistent product master data before activation. 

You can watch the video here: “How-to Video: Creating a Product in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition”. 

Master Data Governance for Products

 

 

Why this matters 
Accurate, governed product data is foundational for downstream processes like sales, procurement, inventory, and analytics. SAP MDG enforces a clear separation of duties, validation checks, and duplicate detection so that master data remains trustworthy across the enterprise. 

 The two-step governance process at a glance 

  • Role split: 
    • Paul (Master Data Requester): Creates and submits the product request 
    • Claire (Master Data Specialist/Approver): Reviews and approves the request 
  • Outcome: Only validated and approved product records become active and available across business processes 

 

 

Result
After approval, the new solar module is active in the system. The controlled process ensures that only high-quality, consistent product master data flows into operational and analytical processes. 

Key takeaways for practitioners 

  • Enforce separation of duties: Separate requester and approver roles reduce risk and increase data quality. 
  • Use process templates: Standardize governance flows for consistent outcomes. 
  • Leverage classification and GTINs: Improve product identification and search, especially across markets and channels. 
  • Validate early, check duplicates: Prevent downstream rework by catching issues before submission. 
  • Monitor outcomes: Use the app Manage Governance Processes – Products to verify process completion and status. 

This example illustrates how SAP MDG on SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition turns a simple product request into governed, reliable master data.
